fields.summary: Joe Biden and Donald Trump face off in a heated 2020 election campaign. Held in the wake of a COVID-19 pandemic and nationwide protests, turnout is expected to be through the roof. Can Joe Biden hold together a large enough coalition of anti-Trump voters to make Trump a one-term President, or will Trump pull of another huge upset after trailing in the polls?

fields.summary:
Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton face off in the 2016 election. While he is well-known among the American public, Trump has never served in elected office. Clinton has served as First Lady, Senator, and Secretary of State. Clinton was the presumptive nominee from start to finish, while Trump has shocked the political world.

How will their campaign play out? Can Trump pull off an upset? Can Clinton continue the legacy of Obama?

Barack Obama attempts to win reelection while Mitt Romney hopes to bring a more conservative vision to the White House. The poor economy and Obama's signature health care initiatives loom large in the 2012 election.

  • Obama will attempt to make the case that his stewardship prevented economic disaster after the 2008 financial crisis.
  • Romney will try to frame his business and executive experience as a contrast to the background and results of Obama.

As the United States heads into the 2008 election, the ongoing war in Iraq continues to divide the public.

  • Barack Obama is a Senator from Illinois and is leading with a message of hope and change.
  • John McCain, Senator from Arizona and Vietnam War hero, takes the Republican mantle from the unpopular George W. Bush.

As an economic crash turns into a deepening recession, many Americans are anxious for a departure from the status quo.

After a close win in 2000, President George Bush has pushed out several controversial policies during his first term. However, the United States is still reeling from 9/11, the first attacks on American soil in decades. All of this means Bush’s reelection will be close.

  • George Bush aims to drum up support for the War on Terror, and motivate his evangelical base.
  • John Kerry aims to emphasize his popular domestic policy, while finessing the issue of terrorism.

George W. Bush attempts to chart a new direction for the U.S., while Al Gore tries to win election as the sitting Vice President. Ralph Nader is a leftist third-party candidate. The economy has been booming, until quite recently, but President Clinton has been through an embarrassing scandal.

The aftershocks of the 1994 Republican Revolution are still reverberating in the 1996 election. With a booming economy, government spending and deficit reduction will be top issues, as well as the conservative “Family Values” culture wars.

  • Bill Clinton attempts to mount a comeback to win a second term by pivoting to the center.
  • Bob Dole seeks to finally claim the White House after a lifetime of public service.
  • Ross Perot hopes to learn from the mistakes of his last third party bid with the new Reform Party.

After eight years of Ronald Reagan, the nation seems headed for a new direction in government.

  • George Bush is Reagan's Vice President, but trails his challenger by several points.
  • Michael Dukakis, Governor of Massachusetts, is a new figure on the national scene. Can he keep the good feelings going through election day?

Bush must find some way to shake up the race. He could emphasize the strong economy, or attack Dukakis on a number of fronts.

fields.summary:
At the outset of the 1984 campaign, the American people don’t seem ready for a change in leadership. President Ronald Reagan benefits from a sense of national prosperity after a rocky start to his term, while Democratic challenger Walter Mondale emerges weakened from a contested Democratic primary after years of carrying water for the unpopular Jimmy Carter.

The ballooning deficit, national defense, and the incumbent’s age are widely acknowledged and controversial issues, but enough Americans feel better than they did four years ago for Reagan to hold the advantage.

  • Ronald Reagan enters the race as the tentative frontrunner, with his sunny optimism and orthodox conservatism growing increasingly palatable to an anxious country.

    • Jimmy Carter faces a tough fight for re-election after a dismal four years.

      • Liberal Republican John Anderson aims to pick off disaffected moderates in both parties.

Jimmy Carter is a new face on the national scene, having served as Governor of Georgia. He will make the case that the nation needs new blood after the scandals of the Nixon era. Both candidates are seen as moderate by the standards of their party. The battleground states are in the West, the Midwest, and the Northeast.

fields.summary:
The 1972 election begins with President Nixon leading in the polls. While he currently has a strong advantage, Richard Nixon has faced criticism over his divisive political style. George McGovern, a liberal Democrat, is widely expected to lose in a landslide. McGovern not only has to heal the wounds of the nation, but also within his party. Some hot issues are wage and price controls, Vietnam, busing, and arms control.

In the real world, the break-in at the Watergate Hotel in June 1972 led to the resignation of Nixon in 1974.

  • Nixon attempts to present himself as a law-and-order candidate who will bear the standard of Republicanism.
  • Humphrey tries to hold the line for liberalism in a year of social chaos and racial agitation.
  • Wallace hopes to bring an end to Civil Rights and desegregation.

fields.summary:
Less than one year after the assassination of John F. Kennedy, America prepares to head to the polls. President Lyndon B. Johnson enters 1964 with the wind on his back, and well into the process of creating his "Great Society." From civil rights to disorder in the streets and Vietnam, LBJ has had to juggle enough for two terms in one year. Now, he must stem the momentum of conservative senator Barry Goldwater, who has overrun the Republican Party.

President Johnson is expected to beat Senator Goldwater in a landslide of historic proportions.

fields.summary:
America in 1964 stands unsettled, memories of the beloved late John F. Kennedy still prominent in the nation's memory. As the nation recovers from the shock of November 1963, the 1964 campaign is just beginning, with questions swirling around America’s course in Vietnam, Social Security, and Civil Rights, among others.
  • Lyndon B. Johnson aims to maintain his large lead in the polls, defending his policies while keeping both integrationist and segregationist voters of the Democratic Party on board.
  • Barry Goldwater hopes to make up ground quickly, reuniting his party behind his conservative vision after a contentious primary, as well as flipping the South for the first time since Reconstruction.

Nixon is the sitting Vice President with a strong Cold War record, moderate economic views, and potential likeability problems. Nixon begins the campaign as the slight favorite, but every region of the country could be competitive. Key issues are the Cold War, civil rights, and health care.

  • Governor Stevenson is an energetic campaigner and a favorite of his party's base, although he is well aware victory is out of the question.

Truman not only has to deal with Dewey, a moderate Republican, but also with two splinter candidates. Henry Wallace is a far-left candidate with the Progressive Party, while Strom Thurmond runs as a Dixiecrat. Some hot issues are the Soviet Union, civil rights, the "Do-Nothing" Congress, and the Taft-Hartley Act.

Wendell Willkie has left the Democratic Party to lead the Republicans against Roosevelt’s unprecedented third term effort.

  • Roosevelt will need to walk the line on foreign policy with an isolationist public, defend his decision to seek a third term, and champion his program of the last 8 years.
  • Willkie must convince and unite a suspicious Republican Party and bring together the internationalist and isolationist wings of his new home against the third term.

The 1876 presidential election season opens with Republican Rutherford Hayes slightly behind Democrat Samuel Tilden as they face off in a high-turnout election. Key issues of this race include reconstruction, tariffs, and corruption, with the shadow of the Grant Administration looming large. The 1828 election will be a rematch between two of the most starkly contrasted personalities in America. General Jackson, a war hero with little formal education, presents himself as the champion of the common man. Meanwhile, President Adams, heir to the country's greatest political dynasty, trades on his reputation as a statesman and intellectual - even if those characteristics aren't doing him much good this year.

Allegations of a corrupt bargain that allowed Adams to win the presidency four years ago are contributing to a fiercely anti-incumbent mood, and mudslinging on both sides abounds.

fields.summary:
The young American Republic roils amid international hostility, growing internal tensions, and questions about the federal government's role in enforcing order and controlling speech.

  • Thomas Jefferson must make the case for a less restrictive federal government while avoiding controversy and fending off various schemes to thwart the democratic process.
  • John Adams must defend the unpopular Alien and Sedition Acts and his negotiations with France without being destroyed by the deep divisions within the Federalist camp.

fields.summary:
The 1968 election reaches its climax with more chaos than ever. Former Vice President Richard Nixon must rebuild the Republican brand four years after Goldwater's disaster. Senator Bobby Kennedy must live up to the lofty rhetoric of his slain brother with more action than words if he is to win back Democratic regulars. George Wallace is an Independent candidate.

Candidates will debate the best course of action on Vietnam, an overheated economy, and the War on Poverty.

fields.summary:
The Articles of Confederation have failed. State governments, anxious to maintain their own power, grant the Congress little respect. The federal government cannot raise funds, cannot resolve its debts, cannot control commerce nor resolve internal disputes. An effort to resolve these deficiencies have resulted not in amendments but an entirely new constitution - not ordained by God, but one drafted, hastily, to address the crisis unfolding.

As critics pick apart the Constitution’s deficiencies, its supporters pin their hopes on one man. They pray that this singular figure may temporarily paper over the Nation’s divisions, and allow not merely ratification but success in a thus-far disappointing experiment in self-governance.

fields.summary:
The Great War grinds on in Europe as America heads to the polls in 1920. President Wilson, diminished by a devastating stroke, seeks vindication for his war policy and his vision of a League of Nations. Theodore Roosevelt has remade himself as the apostle of nationalism, preparedness, and 100% Americanism. Eugene Debs, imprisoned under the Espionage Act for his opposition to the war, runs his campaign from a federal penitentiary in Atlanta.

In the real world, German forces launched the 1918 Spring offensive as their last attempt to rout the Allies before the arrival of American forces. In this world, Germany settled in for a war of attrition, leading President Wilson to seek a third term as a wartime President.

fields.summary:
The depths of the Great Depression have opened up new possibilities in American life. New York Governor and establishment scion Franklin Roosevelt is proposing unprecedented government intervention into the economy, while embattled President Herbert Hoover argues his steady hand is beginning to right the ship.

With one in every four Americans out of work, economic issues are paramount in the 1932 campaign. In the real world, this race was a realignment election, ushering in half a century of Democratic dominance.
